title: Laws, distribution functions, and the Lebesgue integral

sections.title: The law and distribution function of a random variable
paragraphs: Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a random variable. Its law is the probability measure $\mathbb P_X$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B_{\mathbb R})$ defined by $$\mathbb P_X(A)=\mathbb P(\{\omega:X(\omega)\in A\})=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(A)),\qquad A\in\mathcal B_{\mathbb R}.$$ Thus $\mathbb P_X=\mathbb P\circ X^{-1}$, the pushforward of $\mathbb P$ by $X$.
The distribution function, or cumulative distribution function, is $$F_X(t)=\mathbb P_X(( -\infty,t])=\mathbb P(X\le t),\qquad t\in\mathbb R.$$

sections.title: Equality in law and equality almost surely
paragraphs: Write $X\overset{d}=Y$ when $\mathbb P_X=\mathbb P_Y$. Equivalently, $F_X=F_Y$: the sets $(-\infty,t]$ form a generating $\pi$-system, and probability measures agreeing on these sets agree on every Borel set.
Write $X\overset{\mathrm{a.s.}}=Y$ when $\mathbb P(X=Y)=1$, equivalently $\mathbb P((X-Y)^{-1}(\{0\}))=1$. Almost-sure equality implies equality in law.
proof: For $A\in\mathcal B_{\mathbb R}$, $$\{X\in A\}\mathbin{\triangle}\{Y\in A\}\subseteq\{X\ne Y\}.$$ If $X=Y$ almost surely, the symmetric difference is null and therefore $\mathbb P_X(A)=\mathbb P_Y(A)$.

The converse fails. On $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)=((0,1],\mathcal B_{(0,1]},\text{uniform measure})$, take $X(\omega)=\omega$ and $Y(\omega)=1-\omega$. Both have the uniform law on $[0,1]$, but $X=Y$ only when $\omega=1/2$, a null event.

recall.question: Why does $X=Y$ almost surely imply equality in law, and why does the converse fail?
answer: The symmetric difference of the events $\{X\in A\}$ and $\{Y\in A\}$ lies in $\{X\ne Y\}$ for every Borel $A$. For the converse, $X(\omega)=\omega$ and $Y(\omega)=1-\omega$ on the uniform interval have the same law but are unequal almost surely.
checks: Use an arbitrary Borel set, not just a threshold.
Give two variables on the same probability space.

sections.title: Characterizing distribution functions
paragraphs: A function $F:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ is a distribution function if and only if it is nondecreasing, $$\lim_{t\to-\infty}F(t)=0,\qquad \lim_{t\to\infty}F(t)=1,$$ and right-continuous: $$\lim_{s\downarrow t}F(s)=F(t)\quad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.$$
proof: If $F=F_X$, monotonicity follows from inclusion of the events $\{X\le t\}$. The endpoint limits follow from continuity of probability for increasing and decreasing events. In particular, if $t_n\downarrow t$, then $\{X\le t_n\}\downarrow\{X\le t\}$ and hence $F_X(t_n)\downarrow F_X(t)$. The small graph in the notes records the included right endpoint of a jump.
editorial: The handwritten page states the equivalence and sketches the right-continuity direction; it does not contain a converse construction. One converse is to put $U$ uniformly on $(0,1)$ and set $X(U)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge U\}$. Then $\{X\le t\}=\{U\le F(t)\}$, so $F_X=F$. Using $(0,1)$ avoids an infinite value at the null endpoint $U=1$.

sections.title: Almost-sure convergence
paragraphs: A sequence $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ converges almost surely to $X_\infty$, written $X_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}X_\infty$, if $$\mathbb P\bigl(\{\limsup_n X_n=\liminf_n X_n=X_\infty\}\bigr)=1.$$ The limit assertion is a statement about the full path at almost every fixed outcome.
editorial: For finite real-valued limits this is the usual pointwise convergence outside a null event. If infinite limits are allowed, the equality formulation still makes sense; do not use an undefined difference such as $\infty-\infty$.

sections.title: Constructing the Lebesgue integral
paragraphs: For a measure space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu)$ we write $$\mu(f)=\int_\Omega f(\omega)\,\mu(d\omega).$$ Start with nonnegative simple functions $$\mathrm{SF}_+=\left\{\varphi=\sum_{i=1}^{m}c_i\mathbf1_{A_i}:c_i\ge0,\ A_i\in\mathcal F,\ m<\infty\right\},\qquad \mu_0(\varphi)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}c_i\mu(A_i).$$

For a nonnegative measurable $f$, define $$\mu(f)=\sup\{\mu_0(\varphi):\varphi\in\mathrm{SF}_+,\ \varphi\le f\}.$$ For a signed measurable function, put $f_+=\max(f,0)$ and $f_-=\max(-f,0)$, and define $$\mu(f)=\mu(f_+)-\mu(f_-)$$ whenever at least one of the two terms is finite. If both terms are finite, then $f$ is integrable, written $f\in L^1(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu)$.
editorial: The signed definition excludes $\infty-\infty$. Integrability is equivalent to $\mu(|f|)<\infty$. The notes use $\mu(f)$ for an integral as well as $\mu(A)$ for a measure; the argument determines which meaning applies. The course source also permits infinite heights in nonnegative simple functions with $0\cdot\infty=0$; bounded simple functions suffice for the supremum.

sections.title: Why the simple-function integral is well-defined
paragraphs: A simple function can have different representations. Suppose $$\varphi=\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_i\mathbf1_{A_i}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}b_j\mathbf1_{B_j}.$$ We must show $$\sum_i a_i\mu(A_i)=\sum_j b_j\mu(B_j).$$
proof: Refine all of the sets simultaneously. For $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and $T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, let $$Q_{S,T}=\left(\bigcap_{i\in S}A_i\right)\cap\left(\bigcap_{i\notin S}A_i^c\right)\cap\left(\bigcap_{j\in T}B_j\right)\cap\left(\bigcap_{j\notin T}B_j^c\right).$$ These are measurable, pairwise disjoint, and partition $\Omega$; empty intersections mean $\Omega$.

On a nonempty $Q_{S,T}$, both descriptions of $\varphi$ are constant, so $$\varphi|_{Q_{S,T}}=\sum_{i\in S}a_i=\sum_{j\in T}b_j.$$ Finite additivity gives $$\sum_i a_i\mu(A_i)=\sum_{S,T}\left(\sum_{i\in S}a_i\right)\mu(Q_{S,T})=\sum_{S,T}\left(\sum_{j\in T}b_j\right)\mu(Q_{S,T})=\sum_j b_j\mu(B_j).$$ The overlapping-set picture in the notes depicts these common atoms.

The same refinement proves invariance under changes on a null set: if $\mu(\varphi\ne\psi)=0$, then $\mu_0(\varphi)=\mu_0(\psi)$. Combining representations proves $$\mu_0(a\varphi+b\psi)=a\mu_0(\varphi)+b\mu_0(\psi)\quad(a,b\ge0).$$ If $\varphi\le\psi$, the nonnegative simple difference gives $\mu_0(\varphi)\le\mu_0(\psi)$.
editorial: For finite-valued simple functions the difference proof is immediate. If extended heights are allowed, use a common partition and compare its heights directly, avoiding $\infty-\infty$.

sections.title: Integral properties and expectation
paragraphs: For nonnegative measurable functions, the integral is monotone: $f\le g$ implies $\mu(f)\le\mu(g)$. It is positively homogeneous: $\mu(af)=a\mu(f)$ for $a\ge0$. It agrees with the simple integral: $\mu(\varphi)=\mu_0(\varphi)$ for $\varphi\in\mathrm{SF}_+$.

If $f=g$ almost everywhere, then $\mu(f)=\mu(g)$ whenever the integrals are defined. For a simple $\varphi$, monotonicity of $\mu_0$ gives $\mu_0(\psi)\le\mu_0(\varphi)$ for every simple $\psi\le\varphi$, while taking $\psi=\varphi$ gives the reverse inequality in the supremum definition.
On a probability space, the expectation is simply the integral with respect to probability: $$\mathbb E X=\int_\Omega X(\omega)\,\mathbb P(d\omega).$$

sections.title: Monotone convergence and the simple-function lower bound
paragraphs: Monotone convergence: if $h_n$ are nonnegative measurable functions and $h_n\uparrow h$ pointwise, then $$\mu(h_n)\uparrow\mu(h).$$ The value $+\infty$ is allowed.
proof: Monotonicity already gives that $\mu(h_n)$ is nondecreasing and at most $\mu(h)$. It remains to prove the opposite bound for its limit. Fix a nonnegative simple function $\varphi=\sum_{i=1}^{m}c_i\mathbf1_{A_i}\le h$ with disjoint $A_i$, and fix $\lambda\in(0,1)$. The lecture sets $h_*(A_i)=\inf_{\omega\in A_i}h(\omega)$ and compares $c_i\le h_*(A_i)$.

The lecture construction takes $$A_{i,n}=\{\omega\in A_i:h_n(\omega)\ge\lambda h_*(A_i)\},\qquad \varphi_n=\sum_i\lambda h_*(A_i)\mathbf1_{A_{i,n}}\le h_n.$$ For positive finite $h_*(A_i)$, the strict slack $\lambda<1$ and $h_n\uparrow h$ imply $A_{i,n}\uparrow A_i$. Thus $$\lim_n\mu(h_n)\ge\lim_n\mu_0(\varphi_n)=\lambda\sum_i h_*(A_i)\mu(A_i)\ge\lambda\mu_0(\varphi).$$ The drawn step function sits below the limiting curve; each increasing set marks where the current $h_n$ has reached the lowered step.

Let $\lambda\uparrow1$ in this finite-infimum construction to obtain the lower bound $\lim_n\mu(h_n)\ge\mu_0(\varphi)$ for simple functions whose relevant infimum heights are positive and finite. Together with the easy upper bound, this proves that case. The bounded-height construction below supplies the omitted cases and completes the full theorem.
editorial: The handwritten construction does not spell out zero or infinite infimum cases. A uniform repair is to take bounded simple $\varphi$ and instead set $A_{i,n}=\{\omega\in A_i:h_n(\omega)\ge\lambda c_i\}$, omitting zero-height pieces. All thresholds are then finite, $A_{i,n}\uparrow A_i$, and the same argument gives $\lim_n\mu(h_n)\ge\lambda\mu_0(\varphi)$, including infinite measures of pieces. This proves the full statement without dividing by an integral or using an infinite threshold.

recall.question: Reconstruct the proof of monotone convergence. Why is the factor $\lambda<1$ useful?
answer: For bounded simple $\varphi=\sum_i c_i\mathbf1_{A_i}\le h$ with disjoint positive-height pieces, set $A_{i,n}=\{\omega\in A_i:h_n(\omega)\ge\lambda c_i\}$. Strict slack ensures these sets increase to $A_i$ even if $h_n$ approaches the step height only from below. Continuity from below gives $\lim_n\mu(h_n)\ge\lambda\mu_0(\varphi)$. Let $\lambda\uparrow1$ and take the supremum over $\varphi$.
checks: First establish the easy upper bound.
Use continuity from below on sets.

sections.title: Additivity beyond simple functions
proof: The identity already holds for simple functions. Choose nonnegative simple approximations $f_n\uparrow f$ and $g_n\uparrow g$. Then $f_n+g_n\uparrow f+g$, so monotone convergence on each of the three sequences gives $$\mu(f+g)=\lim_n\mu_0(f_n+g_n)=\lim_n\bigl(\mu_0(f_n)+\mu_0(g_n)\bigr)=\mu(f)+\mu(g).$$
editorial: This is the standard approximation pattern: prove a property for indicators/simple functions, then identify the theorem that carries it through a limit. For integrable signed functions, positive/negative decomposition extends linearity after all required finite quantities are checked.

recall.question: Why does simple-function linearity extend to nonnegative measurable functions?
answer: Approximate both functions increasingly by nonnegative simple functions and apply monotone convergence to both approximants and their sums. The finite simple-function identity then passes to the limit.
checks: Their sums must increase to the desired sum.
Name monotone convergence at each passage to a limit.
